topic: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
parentTitle: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
title: Fever in under-5s: the NICE traffic light system
blurb: Measure temperature the right way for age, sort a feverish child into green, amber or red using NICE NG143, and give safe antipyretic advice.
question: Oliver, 7 weeks old, has an axillary temperature of 38.1°C. He is feeding a little less but is pink and settles in his mother's arms. Using the NICE traffic light system, how should his risk be classed?

teach.body: Most fevers in young children are caused by self-limiting viral infections, but a small number signal serious bacterial illness such as sepsis, meningitis or pneumonia. NICE NG143 gives a structured way to spot that minority. Formally, it is a traffic light system that grades the risk of serious illness by colour, activity, respiratory, circulation and hydration, and other signs. Plain English: look at the whole child, not the number on the thermometer, and let the worst feature decide the colour.
teach.cite: NICE NG143 Fever in under 5s (2019, updated 2021)

head: Age
Method
rows: Electronic or chemical dot (axilla), or infra-red tympanic
Do not use forehead chemical strips
teach.caption: A parent's report of fever is valid and should be taken seriously, even if the child is cool now.

rows.label: Activity
values: No smile, wakes with prolonged stimulation
Does not wake or stay awake, weak or high-pitched cry

rows.label: Breathing
values: Nasal flaring, SpO2 95% or less, crackles
Grunting, RR over 60, moderate or severe indrawing

rows.label: Other
values: Fever 5 days or more, rigors, limb swelling
Non-blanching rash, bulging fontanelle, neck stiffness

teach.caption: Green = normal colour, responds normally to social cues, content or smiling, normal skin and eyes, moist mucous membranes, none of the amber or red features.

bands.label: Fever this long: amber, think Kawasaki

teach.caption: Do not use the duration of fever alone, or the response to antipyretics, to judge how ill a child is.

head: Age
Tachycardia (amber)
Tachypnoea (amber)
teach.caption: Capillary refill time of 3 seconds or more is also amber. An RR over 60 at any age under 5 is red.

steps.label: Green
steps.sub: Care at home with safety-netting advice

steps.label: Amber
steps.sub: Safety net or face-to-face review; no diagnosis = clear plan

steps.label: Red
steps.sub: Urgent paediatric assessment; within 2 h if remote and not life-threatening

teach.caption: Life-threatening features (for example compromised airway, shock, unresponsiveness) need emergency care at once.

teach.body: Give paracetamol or ibuprofen if the child appears distressed, not simply to bring the temperature down. Do not give both at the same time. Consider alternating only if distress persists or comes back before the next dose is due. Antipyretics do not prevent febrile seizures. Tepid sponging is not recommended, and the child should not be over- or under-dressed. Offer regular fluids and check on the child during the night.
teach.cite: NICE NG143 recs on antipyretic interventions

teach.text: A fever that comes down with paracetamol does not make the child safe, and a fever that does not come down does not make them sicker. NG143 says response to antipyretics must not be used to judge severity. The traffic light features decide the risk.

teach.h: Scenario: Zara, 4 months, at the walk-in centre
teach.body: Zara has a temperature of 39.3°C. She is alert, pink, feeding normally and has a respiratory rate of 42. Nurse Amina notes that at 3 to 6 months a temperature of 39°C or more is at least amber, whatever the other signs. She records a full set of observations, does not reassure on the basis that Zara looks well, and arranges same-day medical review with clear safety-netting in writing for the parents.

items: Under 4 weeks: electronic axillary thermometer; no forehead strips at any age.
Under 3 months with 38°C or more = red; 3–6 months with 39°C or more = at least amber.
The single worst feature sets the colour: one red feature makes the child red.
Fever for 5 days or more is amber: assess for Kawasaki disease.
Antipyretics for distress only, one at a time; they do not prevent febrile seizures.

summary: You can now measure temperature correctly for age and grade a feverish under-5 as green, amber or red using NG143. You can also give parents accurate advice on antipyretics, fluids and when to seek help again.

A.q: Oliver, 7 weeks old, has an axillary temperature of 38.1°C. He is feeding a little less but is pink and settles in his mother's arms. How is his risk classed under NICE NG143?
options: Green, as he settles easily
Amber, as his feeding is reduced
Red, as he is under 3 months
Amber, as his fever is under 39°C
A.why: Any child under 3 months with a temperature of 38°C or more is in the red (high risk) group, however well they appear.

whyNot.0: Settling well does not lower the risk: age under 3 months with 38°C or more is red on its own.
whyNot.1: Poor feeding is an amber feature, but his age and temperature already place him in red.
whyNot.3: The 39°C threshold applies to babies aged 3 to 6 months, not to those under 3 months.

A.q: Amelia, 2 weeks old, feels hot to her father. Which method should the nurse use to measure her temperature?
options: Infra-red tympanic thermometer
Electronic thermometer in the axilla
Chemical dot thermometer in the axilla
Forehead chemical strip thermometer
A.why: NG143: in babies under 4 weeks, measure temperature with an electronic thermometer in the axilla.

whyNot.0: Infra-red tympanic thermometers are an option from 4 weeks to 5 years, not under 4 weeks.
whyNot.2: Chemical dot axillary thermometers are listed for children from 4 weeks, not newborns.
whyNot.3: Forehead chemical thermometers are unreliable and should not be used at any age.

A.q: Poppy, 2, has a temperature of 38.7°C and is playing happily. Her mother asks whether she should give paracetamol to bring the temperature down. What is the best advice?
options: Give paracetamol and ibuprofen together
Give paracetamol to help prevent a febrile seizure
Give paracetamol now and then every 4 hours
Use an antipyretic if Poppy becomes distressed
A.why: Antipyretics are for a child who is distressed by the fever, not to reduce temperature in a child who is comfortable.

whyNot.0: NG143 advises against giving both agents at the same time.
whyNot.1: Antipyretics do not prevent febrile seizures and should not be given for that reason.
whyNot.2: Regular dosing to keep the temperature down is not the aim when the child is comfortable.

B.q: Kian, 2, has a temperature of 38.9°C. He responds to his parents but is not smiling, his heart rate is 145 and his capillary refill time is 2 seconds. What is his traffic light category?
options: Green, because his capillary refill time is normal
Amber, because of his tachycardia and no smile
Red, because his heart rate is over 140
Green, because he responds to his parents
B.why: No smile is an amber activity feature, and a heart rate over 140 at 2 to 5 years is amber tachycardia. No red features are present.

whyNot.0: A normal capillary refill does not cancel his amber features.
whyNot.2: A heart rate over 140 at this age is an amber, not a red, feature.
whyNot.3: Responding to parents is reassuring, but not smiling is still amber.

B.q: Leo, 2, has had a fever for 6 days. His mother says it keeps coming back despite paracetamol. He has red eyes and cracked lips. What should the nurse recognise?
options: Fever of 5 days or more needs Kawasaki assessment
Failure to respond to paracetamol makes him high risk
A viral illness is likely after this long
His fever becomes amber once it reaches 39°C
B.why: Fever lasting 5 days or more is an amber feature, and NG143 says to assess for Kawasaki disease (red eyes and cracked lips fit).

whyNot.1: Response to antipyretics should not be used to judge severity.
whyNot.2: Prolonged fever is a warning sign, not reassurance that the illness is viral.
whyNot.3: Duration of 5 days or more is amber in its own right; 39°C is the amber threshold for babies aged 3 to 6 months.

B.q: Ravi, 3, has a fever. His father has been sponging him with lukewarm water and wrapping him in extra blankets. What should the nurse advise?
options: Continue sponging and add a fan
Stop sponging and dress him normally
Keep the blankets on to prevent shivering
Sponge him with cold water instead
B.why: NG143 does not recommend tepid sponging, and children with fever should be neither over-wrapped nor under-dressed.

whyNot.0: Tepid sponging is not recommended for fever.
whyNot.2: Over-wrapping a feverish child is advised against.
whyNot.3: Cold sponging is more uncomfortable and is not recommended either.

C.q: Isla, 11 months, has a fever of 38.5°C. She is pink and alert, but her respiratory rate is 54 with nasal flaring, and SpO2 is 96% in air. Her mother says she is drinking less. What is the most appropriate plan?
options: Green: home care, no follow-up
Emergency transfer as she is red
Face-to-face review with a safety net
Give paracetamol and recheck in 4 hours
C.why: RR over 50 at 6 to 12 months, nasal flaring and poor feeding are amber features. Amber needs face-to-face assessment and a clear safety net.

whyNot.0: She is not green: RR over 50 at 6 to 12 months, nasal flaring and poor feeding are amber, so she needs face-to-face assessment or a safety net.
whyNot.1: There are no red features such as grunting, RR over 60 or a mottled skin.
whyNot.3: Response to an antipyretic does not settle amber risk, and the plan delays assessment.

C.q: Mia, 14 months, has a fever. She is pink and her rash blanches, but she has a bulging fontanelle and a weak, high-pitched cry. What is her category and response?
options: Amber: review within 24 hours
Green: the rash is blanching
Amber: oral fluids and a safety net
Red: urgent paediatric assessment
C.why: A bulging fontanelle and a weak, high-pitched cry are both red features, so she needs urgent assessment by a paediatric specialist.

whyNot.0: Both features are red, not amber, and need urgent review, not within 24 hours.
whyNot.1: A blanching rash does not exclude meningitis when red neurological features are present.
whyNot.2: Oral fluids and safety-netting are the response to amber features, not red ones.

C.q: Ellie, 18 months, has amber features but no diagnosis has been made. The doctor plans to send her home. What should the nurse make sure the parents receive?
options: A clear written safety net and when to return
Ibuprofen to give at the first sign of fever
Advice to wake her for paracetamol doses overnight
A note to return if fever lasts over 10 days
C.why: NG143: amber with no diagnosis can go home with a safety net: written and verbal advice on warning signs and how to get further care, or a follow-up appointment.

whyNot.1: Antipyretics are for distress, not to treat the first sign of fever.
whyNot.2: Antipyretics are given for distress, not on a schedule; NG143 asks parents to check on the child during the night, not to wake her for doses.
whyNot.3: Fever of 5 days or more is already amber, so 10 days is far too long to wait.

reteach.title: Let the worst sign choose the colour
reteach.question: If a feverish toddler has nine reassuring features and one red one, which colour are they?

blocks.body: Think of the traffic light like a set of locks: one locked door stops you. Work through colour, activity, breathing, circulation and hydration, and other signs. If any single feature is red, the child is red. If none is red but one is amber, the child is amber. Only a child with no amber or red features is green. Age and temperature can be a feature by themselves under 6 months.

blocks.text: Looking well does not override age: a baby under 3 months with 38°C or more is red even if pink, feeding and settled.

explain.body: Under 4 weeks: electronic thermometer in the axilla. From 4 weeks to 5 years: electronic or chemical dot in the axilla, or infra-red tympanic. Forehead strips are not used. If a parent says the child had a fever, believe them.

test.q: A parent says her 3-year-old was hot overnight, but his temperature in clinic is 37.2°C. How should the nurse treat the report?
options: As unreliable until confirmed
As valid evidence of fever
As amber because it was overnight
As red because it was not measured
test.why: NG143 says reported parental perception of fever should be taken seriously and treated as valid.

whyNot.0: Parental report is accepted as valid, not discounted.
whyNot.2: Timing overnight is not an amber feature.
whyNot.3: An unmeasured fever is not in itself a red feature.

explain.body: Under 3 months with 38°C or more is red. Aged 3 to 6 months with 39°C or more is at least amber. Fever lasting 5 days or more is amber, and Kawasaki disease should be considered.

test.q: Alfie, 5 months, has a temperature of 39.1°C and no other abnormal signs. What is the minimum category?
options: Green
Red
Amber
Green if feeding well
test.why: A temperature of 39°C or more at 3 to 6 months is at least amber.

whyNot.0: His age and temperature mean he cannot be green.
whyNot.1: Red applies to under 3 months with 38°C or more, or to red clinical features.
whyNot.3: Good feeding does not lower the age-based amber threshold.

explain.body: Red: pale, mottled, ashen or blue; does not wake or stay awake; weak, high-pitched or continuous cry; grunting; RR over 60; moderate or severe chest indrawing; reduced skin turgor; non-blanching rash; bulging fontanelle; neck stiffness; status epilepticus; focal neurology or focal seizures.

letters.word: Activity: will not wake, weak cry

test.q: Which finding in a feverish 2-year-old is a red feature?
options: Dry mucous membranes
Nasal flaring
Grunting
Capillary refill of 3 seconds
test.why: Grunting is a red respiratory feature in NG143.

whyNot.0: Dry mucous membranes are an amber hydration feature.
whyNot.1: Nasal flaring is an amber respiratory feature.
whyNot.3: A capillary refill of 3 seconds or more is amber.

explain.body: Paracetamol or ibuprofen for distress, not for the number. Do not give both together; alternate only if distress persists or recurs before the next dose. They do not prevent febrile seizures. No tepid sponging; offer regular fluids.

test.q: Ibuprofen settled Jack's distress, but 2 hours later he is miserable again and the next dose is not due. What does NG143 allow?
options: Consider giving paracetamol instead
Give a second ibuprofen dose early
Give both drugs together from now on
Start tepid sponging until it is due
test.why: If distress persists or recurs before the next dose is due, alternating to the other agent can be considered.

whyNot.1: Giving ibuprofen early exceeds the dosing interval.
whyNot.2: Both agents should not be given at the same time.
